The SPPT report also called for the RSC to establish the Highway/Byway cost allocation method for all new regional transmission facilities and to determine whether to use the new Highway/Byway cost allocation proposal for the Priority Projects.19 The justification for the recommendation of a new cost allocation method was twofold. First, the SPPT noted that SPP was currently using three different methods for different project planning processes, including separate rates for zonal projects and regional projects, a postage stamp rate for Balance Portfolio projects, and a new yet-to-be-determined rate for extra-high-voltage overlay projects. The SPPT report (SPP 2009) continued, “SPP members and staff have expressed concern that these cost recovery methods are fragmented, confusing, and difficult to administer as it requires a complex system to track cost by project over the life of the project… the SPPT recommends expanding and including a comprehensive review of all cost allocation methodologies for possible consolidation under a unified system using the recommended ‘highway-byway’ approach.” Second, the SPPT determined that postage stamp cost allocation “tends to support robust regional projects” and that a Highway/Byway method based on a voltage limit would convince some SPP members who did not support a traditional postage stamp rate. SPP justified the new Highway/Byway cost allocation method to FERC by citing previous studies that explored the power flow dynamics of high-voltage transmission facilities compared to lower-voltage transmission facilities throughout the SPP footprint.20 One such study was a transmission distribution analysis, which analyzes the power flow response of transmission facilities at different voltages across the footprint to assess which facilities are responsible for regional power flows and which are used primarily for local power flows (SPP 2010d).
